name: Pigeonhole principle
formula: n \text{ objects in } k \text{ boxes} \implies \text{some box holds at least } \left\lceil \frac{n}{k} \right\rceil
whenToUse: Questions asking for the fewest picks that GUARANTEE something, or a proof that two things must share a property.
example: A drawer holds socks in $5$ colours. To guarantee $3$ of one colour, $2 \cdot 5 = 10$ socks are not enough (two of each), but $11$ are.
pitfall: Build the worst case explicitly: the most objects you can take WITHOUT the property, then add one. Read whether the problem wants a guarantee or just a possibility.
